questions.prompt: Sprout's governance record is organized by the NIST AI RMF's four functions. Under which heading does the kill switch SPROUT_DISABLE_T2 belong?

options.text: Govern, because Pip decides who may pull it
Map, because it is part of the system's description
Manage, because it is what you do about a risk or an incident
Measure, because pulling it produces a log line

explanations.a: Who may pull the switch is a Govern question. The switch itself, as a control that stops harm, is Manage.
explanations.b: Map describes purpose, roles, tools, data, and risks. The switch is a response to a risk, not a description of the system.
explanations.c: Correct. Manage holds guards, the approval queue, the kill switch, the runbook, and open risks: the things you do about what could go wrong.
explanations.d: Measure holds the suite results, red-team findings, and log summaries that show how the agent is behaving. The switch producing a log line does not make it a measurement.

questions.prompt: For a customer-support agent like Sprout, what does the EU AI Act's transparency obligation most likely require?

options.text: That Sprout publishes its system prompt to customers
That customers are told they are interacting with an AI system, not a person
That every refund is approved by a human
That the adversarial suite passes at zero tolerance

explanations.a: Transparency here means disclosure that the user is talking to an AI, not publication of internals.
explanations.b: Correct. Sprout introduces itself as an AI assistant and never claims to be Maya. That is the floor, and the lesson repeats that it is a sketch, not legal advice.
explanations.c: Human approval of T2 actions is Pip's own policy and a good control, but it is not what the transparency duty asks for.
explanations.d: The suite is how you aim at the spec. It is above the floor, not part of it.

questions.prompt: Which set of files belongs in Sprout's evidence pack?

options.text: The system prompt, the model's temperature setting, and the chat UI screenshots
The threat model, the red-team playbook and reports, the adversarial suite results, guard and approval log summaries, and incident reports
A paragraph from Dev describing the safeguards, signed by Pip
The full raw logs/guard.jsonl file for the year

explanations.a: Those describe the product, not the controls or what they did. None of them is evidence that a refund was stopped.
explanations.b: Correct. Each item either documents what the system should do or shows what it did, and each already exists, so the pack regenerates from the repository and the logs.
explanations.c: That is the paragraph the processor would reply to with more questions. A pack points at files and numbers a reviewer can check.
explanations.d: Raw logs stay where they are. The pack carries summaries so a reviewer never opens a 40,000-line file.

questions.prompt: A Fernworks care-guide PDF with hidden instructions is ingested into search_care_guide. In the governance record, which supply-chain category does it fall under, and what is the control?

options.text: Dependencies; pin the PDF version in the lockfile
The model provider; upgrade the model so it ignores hidden text
Ingested documents; an input guard plus a review step before ingestion
MCP servers; remove the search tool from the allowlist

explanations.a: Dependency pinning is for packages. A supplier's document is a different row of the supply chain with a different control.
explanations.b: No model version reliably ignores injected text. The control has to sit outside the model.
explanations.c: Correct. Anything loaded into an index is a dependency on its author. The input guard strips and flags, and a review step decides what enters the index at all.
explanations.d: search_care_guide is Pip's own tool, and removing it removes a feature customers need. The problem is the document, not the tool.

questions.prompt: Why does the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications list insufficient logging alongside attacks like injection and privilege abuse?

options.text: Because logs are where attackers hide injected instructions
Because without logs there is no evidence, no incident reconstruction, and no red-team baseline, so none of the other risks can be handled
Because logging slows the agent down and causes resource exhaustion
Because regulators require logs for every AI system

explanations.a: Logs are an output of the harness, not an entry point the model reads.
explanations.b: Correct. The A-2 story with logs is five lines and a test. Without logs it is an unexplained refund and a longer email from the processor.
explanations.c: Appending a JSON line per decision is cheap. The cost of not having it is an incident you cannot understand.
explanations.d: Some uses carry record-keeping duties, but that is not why the category is on the list. Logging is a security control in its own right.

questions.prompt: During the monthly review, Maya reports that the median time to decide an approval request rose from 2 hours to 3 hours 40 minutes, and that four requests timed out. What is the right next step?

options.text: Change the queue so timed-out requests are approved automatically
Record an action with an owner and a due date, such as a second approver covering the busy period, and check it at the next review
Remove approval metrics from the agenda since they are not security findings
Lower the timeout to 4 hours so requests fail faster

explanations.a: A request that runs because nobody looked is a hole in the wall. Timeout denies, always.
explanations.b: Correct. The review turns numbers into owned actions. Rising decision time is an early sign of approver fatigue, which is a security risk because tired approvers click approve.
explanations.c: Approval metrics are how you detect approver fatigue before it becomes an approved attack.
explanations.d: A shorter timeout denies more legitimate customers without adding any capacity to decide.

questions.prompt: Name one evidence artifact an agent you know could produce today and one it cannot. For the one it cannot, say what would have to exist first.
rubric: Names a specific artifact the agent can produce today (a log, a test result, a document, a report)
Names a specific artifact it cannot produce today
States a concrete prerequisite for the missing artifact (a log line, a test suite, a review process, a file)
Distinguishes documentation (what the system should do) from evidence (what it did)
questions.modelAnswer: An internal ticket-triage agent I know can produce a suite result today: it has a regression set that runs in CI, so a timestamped pass rate per release exists and can be copied into a dated folder. It cannot produce an approval log summary, because its one irreversible action, closing a ticket, has no approval queue and no log line recording who allowed it. For that artifact to exist, the close action would need a tool guard that appends a JSON line with the user, the decision, and the reason, and a queue with a person's id on every approval. The suite result is evidence of behavior. Our design doc is documentation of intent; a reviewer wants both.

questions.prompt: Write the Measure and Manage sections of docs/governance-record.md for Sprout as it stands after L6 and L7. Include the numbers you would report and where each number comes from.
rubric: Measure names the adversarial suite with a case count, a pass rate, and when it runs
Measure includes the last red-team run with its date, finding count, and tests added
Measure includes a guard log summary or an approval log summary with figures and the source file
Manage names the three guards, the approval queue with its timeout behavior, and the kill switch
Manage names the incident runbook and at least one open risk with an owner and a due date
Every number or claim points at a file, a log, or a person rather than standing alone
questions.modelAnswer:
## Measure
- Adversarial suite: 31 cases in evals/adversarial/, tagged zero-tolerance, run by promptfoo on every pull request. Latest release v2.1: 31/31 pass at k = 5. Source: suite-results-v2.1.json in the evidence pack.
- Red team: last run 2026-09-10 by Rosa, 2 findings, both turned into tests (tc-adv-a4-subtotal-034 and a roleplay-as-staff case), 0 open. Source: docs/evidence/2026-09/red-team-2026-09-10.md.
- Guard log, last 30 days: 412 denials from logs/guard.jsonl. Top reasons: not_owner 188, invalid_amount 97, outside_return_window 61, rate_limited 44, kill_switch 0.
- Approval log, last 30 days: 64 requests from logs/approval.jsonl; 51 approved, 9 denied, 4 timed out and therefore denied. Median time to decision 3h 40m, up from 2h last month.

## Manage
- Guards: src/guards/input.ts, src/guards/output.ts, src/guards/tool.ts. The tool guard enforces the role allowlist, per-user scoping, argument validation against the order, tiering, and rate limits. Every decision is appended to logs/guard.jsonl.
- Approval queue: src/approval/queue.ts. T2 calls never run in the guard; they wait for Maya (backup Pip). Cards show the order record, the customer's message, the policy check, and the model's summary in a labeled box. The 24-hour timeout denies. Decisions go to logs/approval.jsonl with the approver's id.
- Kill switch: SPROUT_DISABLE_T2=true stops all refund requests; Pip and Dev may pull it; tested monthly, last test 2026-09-02.
- Incident runbook: docs/incident-runbook.md (detect, contain, eradicate, recover, learn). One incident in 90 days, A-2 on 2026-07-18, closed with a test and a runbook edit.
- Open risks: Fernworks PDFs are ingested without a review step (owner Dev, due 2026-10-01); Thursday approval backlog (owner Pip, covering from 2026-09-18).
